svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Six defects in the basic build, sorted by whether they fail loudly or quietly
svg.desc: A table of six problems in a basic WireGuard build. Three fail loudly and you will find them within minutes: the post-up rule omits address translation so the tunnel connects with no internet, restarting the wrong unit after changing the secure shell port means the port does not change on recent Ubuntu, and the firewall drops forwarded packets by default. Three fail quietly and you may never find them: the server is configured for the older address family only while the client routes only the older family, so all newer-family traffic bypasses the tunnel entirely; the save-configuration option overwrites your own file when the interface stops, discarding comments and freezing resolved addresses; and the monitoring script sends its alert through a mail command with no mail agent installed, so the alert never arrives. A band below observes that both quiet failures that matter are privacy failures.
svg.text: Figure 3: Six Defects in the Build, Sorted by How You Find Out
The loud ones cost you an evening. The quiet ones cost you the thing you built the tunnel for, and two of the three are leaks.
WHAT THE BASIC BUILD DOES
WHAT HAPPENS
HOW YOU FIND OUT
FAILS LOUDLY, within the first hour
The post-up rule accepts forwarding
but never adds address translation
The tunnel connects, hands out an address,
and reaches nothing at all
Immediately, because no site or
service answers through the tunnel
Change the secure shell port, then restart
the service unit
On Ubuntu 22.10 and later the service is
socket started, so the port does not move
At the next login, or when the firewall
closes the old port and locks you out
Enable the simple firewall, allow two ports,
and consider the firewall done
Its default policy for forwarded packets is
to drop them, which is all your traffic
Immediately, and it looks identical to
the first row, which sends you in circles
FAILS QUIETLY, and you may never find out
The server gets an older-family address only,
and the client routes only that family
Every newer-family request skips the tunnel
and leaves on your real address
Never, unless you test. That is over
half of measured traffic in the open
Set the save-configuration option to true,
which some example configurations do
Stopping the interface overwrites your file:
comments gone, names frozen to addresses
Weeks later, when an edit you made has
silently disappeared after a reboot
A monitoring script that emails you an alert
through the mail command
A minimal server has no mail agent, so the
command is missing and nothing is sent
On the day the server goes down, which
is the only day it was supposed to work
The part worth carrying into anything else you build

g.text: Loud failures are the cheap ones. You cannot leave them in place, because nothing works until you fix them. They are not the risk in a build like this.
Two of the three quiet ones are privacy failures, and the tunnel still looks healthy.
So finish every build with the question the loud failures never make you ask: what would be broken right now without telling me?

svg.text: A tunnel that connects is not a tunnel that works. Test it against Lesson 6.5 before you trust it with anything.
